conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure moms get the support they need after baby arrives. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question tool that helps us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything stays confidential, and we can pause any time. When you’re ready, we’ll just talk through the questions together.

To start: Over the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you used to, or has that been harder lately?
Hi Sarah, thank you. I’ve still been enjoying most things—maybe just in shorter bursts because I’m tired, but I can still laugh at my favorite show and feel happy when the baby smiles at me.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I’ve still been laughing—maybe not quite as loudly or as often, but when my partner cracks a joke or I watch a silly video while I’m feeding her, I’ll still chuckle.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to little things—like my morning coffee once she’s settled in her bouncer or the short walk we take most afternoons—but the excitement feels quieter than before. It’s more “that’ll be nice” than “I can’t wait,” if that makes sense.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, if she spits up a ton after I feed her, I might think “oops, maybe I burped her wrong,” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I just clean us up and try a different hold next time.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Sometimes I’ll suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds normal or if the room’s too cool, even though everything checks out. It’s not all day—just quick flashes of worry that pass once I peek at her or adjust the monitor.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like panic. I get those quick “what-if” worries, but they never turn into real fear or a racing heart. It’s more a brief flutter and then I’m okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like when she’s fussy and the laundry’s piled up, I’ll feel a wave of “how am I going to do all this?” But once she naps or my partner takes over for a bit, I can tackle things again. It doesn’t feel unmanageable for long.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s actually been fine—well, as fine as it can be with a newborn. Once I lie down, I’m out pretty quickly. I don’t stay awake feeling unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I get tired and a little overwhelmed sometimes, but I wouldn’t call it sad. I still smile when she grabs my finger or when my older dog curls up next to us.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried at all this week. I might feel a bit teary when I’m really tired, but the tears never actually come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [enter date]  
Source: Self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  

A. Positive Findings  
- Mild, situational “quick-flash” worries about infant well-being (Q4)  
- Episodic sense of being “overwhelmed” when infant is fussy and chores pile up; resolves with support/infant sleep (Q6)  

B. Negative / Low-risk Findings  
- Denies persistent low mood, crying spells, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Denies guilt, self-blame beyond ordinary parenting adjustments (Q3)  
- Denies panic, nocturnal mood-related insomnia, self-harm ideation (Q5, Q7, Q10)  
- Maintains capacity for pleasure and humour, albeit “quieter” than pre-pregnancy (Q1, Q2)  

C. Pattern Summary  
Transient anxiety and manageable overwhelm in context of new parenting demands; no evidence of major depressive or anxiety episode on screening.  

D. Risk Level  
Current responses place patient below conventional cut-off for high postpartum depression risk; no safety concerns identified. Continue routine support and re-screen if clinical picture changes.
